newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Vale's long-term outlook seen bright.
newsitem.headline: Vale's long-term outlook seen bright.

text.p: Brazilian mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce is correctly valued at about 10 billion reais and its bright long-term outlook bodes well for the company's stock, analysts said.
"What I see for this company is a very good prospect in the long term," said Roberto Dotta, an analyst at Indosuez in Brazil. "There's great potential for the company after privatization," he added.

Shares of Vale, one of the world's largest iron producers with an array of other interests, jumped 15 percent to 20 percent after the government earlier this month announced its three-phase privatization model for the company.
The selloff, slated to begin in February 1997, will be one of Latin America's largest privatizations to date.
Brasilia has not released a base price.

But National Development Bank (BNDES) chief Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros last week said gains in Vale's preferred and ordinary shares after the government's Sept 5 announcement boosted the total market value of the firm to 10 billion reais from 8.2 billion reais.
Meanwhile, a tax exemption for exports signed into law last week will add another 600 million reais to Vale's total worth, analysts said.
The market is now fairly valuing Vale stock in light of its virtually assured privatization and does not foresee a significant short-term move in share prices, analysts said.
"Ten billion is about what the market is expecting," said Steven Assis, an analyst at Nomura Securities in New York.
"Some banks saw it as higher, but that's close to most projections," said Aymar Almeada of Bank of Boston's local branch.
But many analysts are still studying the impact of the ICMS tax reduction and declined to offer a year-end price estimate for Vale shares.
"The stock price does not fully reflect the change in the tax rule," added Assis.
Analysts said the exemption would add between $36 million and $75 million to the firm's annual revenues.
Apart from being a mining conglomerate, Vale also operates rail lines and ports and produces aluminum.

There is ample reason to be upbeat about the company's long-term outlook, especially after privatization, as mining and non-mining costs are reduced and the firm is allowed to invest outside Brazil, analysts said.
Private management is seen placing greater emphasis on gold, silver and copper projects, which offer better prospects for revenue growth than iron ore, analysts said.
But it is difficult to project a short-term share price hike. "Vale is a very complex company," said Renato Tranjan of Rio-based Banco Omega.
Any hike will depend on whether the government places a fair base price on Vale shares in its initial auction of a 40-45 percent controlling stake as well as competition during the bidding, he said.
Tranjan projects the firm will end 1996 with a $215 million net profit this year versus $337.9 million last year, a decline mostly due to stronger dollar and lower world iron ore prices.
-- James Craig, Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 232 4411
